Base directory for this skill: D:\oh-my-posh\.claude\skills\code-changes

# Code Changes

The workflow for going from an issue, pull request, idea, or feature request to shipped code.
Follow the phases in order. Analysis always comes first; code comes last.

Each phase has a reference file with the full instructions. **Read the reference file when you
enter the phase** — not before, and never skip it because the phase "looks obvious".

## Roles

Assign work based on model capability. The coordinator is not the strongest model — it's the one
that stays resident, owns every phase by default, and knows when it's out of its depth.

| Role        | Capability tier                                               | Owns                                                                          |
| ----------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Coordinator | Capable mid-tier, resident for the whole task                | Analysis, plan, delegation, supervision, verification, delivery — by default |
| Escalation  | Strongest reasoning model available; invoked only on trigger | The specific judgment call the coordinator flagged, then control returns     |
| Implementer | Same tier as coordinator, or smaller for trivial edits        | Executing one pinned, self-contained task                                    |

Concrete model names per vendor (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google) and how to run the split in Claude
Code, GitHub Copilot, Codex, or IDE agents: [references/model-tiers.md](references/model-tiers.md).

When the current agent already runs at implementer tier, there's no separate delegation step for
standard work: plan and execute directly, still following every phase. Escalate to the strongest
model only when a trigger fires — see [references/escalate.md](references/escalate.md) — never by
default and never for a routine judgment call the coordinator is equipped to make itself.

## The flow

1. **Analyze** ([references/analyze.md](references/analyze.md)) — root cause and scope,
   validated against the code, never against the report alone.
2. **Plan** ([references/plan.md](references/plan.md)) — pinned spec, task split, parallel vs
   sequential, workspace per task.
3. **Delegate** ([references/delegate.md](references/delegate.md)) — match each task to the
   right executor, coordinator-tier by default.
4. **Supervise** ([references/supervise.md](references/supervise.md)) — monitor, unblock, and
   critically review implementer output.
5. **Verify** ([references/verify.md](references/verify.md)) — quality gates plus functional
   proof, never delegated downward.
6. **Deliver** ([references/deliver.md](references/deliver.md)) — conventional commits and an
   outcome-first report.

Analyze, Supervise, and Verify each carry an escalation checkpoint — see
[references/escalate.md](references/escalate.md) — for handing one specific judgment call to the
strongest available model without giving up ownership of the phase.

**Stop gate:** Phase 1 ends with reporting the analysis and proposed approach to the user and
waiting for a go. Skip the gate only when the user already gave the go in the request itself
("do it", "fix it and commit", "implement with Sonnet").

## Special cases

These entry points replace or extend Phase 1; the rest of the flow applies unchanged.

- Pull request review comments →
  [references/pr-review-comments.md](references/pr-review-comments.md)
- Issue triage → [references/issue-triage.md](references/issue-triage.md)

Research the current (2026) web design and information architecture of developer/CLI tool marketing + docs websites. Use WebSearch and WebFetch heavily.

Target sites to analyze in depth (fetch the actual pages, don't guess from memory):
1. starship.rs — the direct competitor to Oh My Posh (a cross-shell prompt engine)
2. zed.dev
3. bun.sh (or bun.com)
4. biomejs.dev
5. astro.build
6. tauri.app
7. warp.dev
8. ghostty.org
9. atuin.sh
10. charm.sh / charm.land (Bubble Tea, Glow etc.)
11. fig.io if reachable, and mise.jdx.dev, uv (docs.astral.sh/uv), ruff

For EACH site report concretely:
- Homepage above-the-fold structure: headline wording, subhead, primary/secondary CTA, hero visual type (static screenshot, animated terminal, video, asciinema-style replay, live interactive demo)
- Navigation architecture: top-level nav items, whether docs are sidebar-first or landing-page-first, how installation is surfaced, how a "reference" (options/segments/config) section is organized, search placement
- Visual language: color palette (list hex codes if you can extract them), typography (font families), dark/light default, use of gradients/glass/noise/grain, border radius language, motion
- Doc site tech (Docusaurus / VitePress / Nextra / Starlight / custom / Mintlify)
- What is genuinely good and worth stealing; what is dated

Then produce a synthesis:
- The 3-4 dominant design idioms in 2026 dev-tool sites
- Common navigation patterns for tools with a LARGE reference surface (many config options / plugins / segments) — how do they keep it navigable? (tabs, grouped sidebar, searchable index grid, cards, filterable catalog)
- Specific patterns for "theme gallery" / "showcase" pages
- Anti-patterns to avoid

Be concrete and cite URLs. Return a dense structured report, no fluff. This is for a redesign proposal, so specificity beats breadth.

Map the complete information architecture of the Oh My Posh website located at D:\oh-my-posh\website (Docusaurus 3 site).

Do all of this by reading files (do NOT modify anything):
1. Read website/sidebars.js in full and reproduce the exact sidebar tree (categories and doc ids, in order).
2. List every file under website/docs with its path, and for each, its frontmatter `id`, `title`, and `sidebar_label` if present. Group by directory (installation/, configuration/, segments/, advanced/, contributing/, plus root-level docs).
3. Count how many segment docs exist under website/docs/segments and list them grouped by their subdirectory.
4. Read website/src/pages/index.js and website/src/pages/styles.module.css in full and describe the current homepage: sections, copy, CTAs, imagery.
5. Read website/src/css/custom.css in full and extract: the color variables used, fonts, any custom component styling, notable overrides.
6. Read website/src/components/Config.js and Auth.js and explain what they render.
7. List website/blog contents (post titles + dates).
8. Note anything in website/static that matters for design (hero.png, logos, theme screenshots count, accordeon.png etc).
9. Check website/plugins/ for what the appinsights plugin does.
10. Report any obvious IA problems you notice: deep nesting, ambiguous category names, docs that are hard to find, duplicated entry points, missing landing pages for categories.

Return a dense, structured report. Include the full sidebar tree verbatim — it is the most important artifact. No fluff.

**Current state — Docusaurus scaffold, barely touched since 2020**
- [index.js](website/src/pages/index.js) is the stock template: centered hero, 3 emoji feature cards, 2 buttons. No install command, no live demo, no social proof, no stats.

- `Get Started →` goes to `/docs/`, which renders **Configuration → Introduction** — theory about blocks/segments, not install. Wrong first click.
- Themes page: 124 PNGs, 28,093px tall, 8MB, no filter/search/tags.
- 117 segment docs in 8 groups — the biggest reference surface, buried in one collapsed sidebar node.
- [custom.css](website/src/css/custom.css) has hardcoded CSS-module hashes (`a.getStarted_Sjon`, `.themedImage_ToTc`) — brittle. Fira Code fetched from Google Fonts and never used.

**Competitor snapshot (measured, not recalled)**
- starship.rs: VitePress, dark default `#1b1b1f`, Inter, nav = **one item** (Configuration) + language picker, single CTA.
- ghostty.org: `#0f0f11`, custom variable font, 6px radius.

content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme: `prefers-color-scheme` carries the OS preference, and the viewer's toggle stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, which must override the media query in both directions. The robust pattern is token-level: define the palette as custom properties on `:root`, redefine only the tokens under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` — style components through the tokens, never directly inside the media query — then redefine them again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` and `:root[data-theme="light"]`. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

# 2026 Dev-Tool Site Research — Marketing + Docs IA

Methodology note: WebFetch converts to Markdown (strips CSS), so palettes/fonts were extracted separately from raw HTML and stylesheet downloads. Two caveats flagged inline: **ghostty.org's homepage is fully client-rendered and its `<main>` stayed empty in a headless browser** (only shell tokens recoverable), and **fig.io is dead** (Fig sunset 2024-09-01, redirected into Amazon Q Developer CLI — remove it from any competitive set).

---

## 1. starship.rs — the direct competitor

**Above the fold** (https://starship.rs/)
- Hero is the **stock VitePress `layout: home`**: centered `logo.svg`, tagline *"The minimal, blazing-fast, and infinitely customizable prompt for any shell!"*, single action button **"Get Started →"** → `/guide/`.
- **No hero screenshot, no terminal demo, no animation.** For a product whose entire value is visual, this is the single biggest miss.
- Three VitePress feature cards: *Compatibility First* / *Rust-Powered* / *Customizable*.
- Below fold: **Prerequisites** (Nerd Font) then **Quick Install** — install commands and per-shell init snippets for 11 shells inlined directly on the homepage. Effectively the homepage *is* the getting-started page.

**Navigation**: `Configuration` · `Advanced Configuration` · `FAQ` · `Presets` · language switcher (13 locales) · GitHub · appearance toggle. Docs are **landing-page-first for install, sidebar-first thereafter**. Search: Algolia DocSearch in the header (`⌘K`), confirmed in markup.

**Visual language** (extracted from `/assets/style.DFqZBrzq.css`)
- Brand: light `--vp-c-brand-1: #dd0b78`, `-2: #f31186`, `-3: #9b0854`; dark `#ff33b8` / `#ff14ad` / `#ff70cd`. Magenta/pink on otherwise stock VitePress neutrals (`--vp-c-bg: #ffffff` / dark `#1b1b1f`, `--vp-c-bg-alt: #161618`).
- Type: `Inter` for body; **mono stack is prefixed with `"Nerd Font"`** — a nice touch, glyphs in code blocks render correctly.
- Syntax theme in the raw HTML is GitHub-dark-ish: `#9ecbff`, `#b392f0`, `#79b8ff`, `#f97583`, `#6a737d`.
- Dark/light toggle, system default. No gradients, no glass, no grain, no motion. VitePress default radii.

**Doc tech**: VitePress (`#VPContent`, `--vp-*` tokens, `/vp-icons.css`).

**Reference surface**: https://starship.rs/config/ is **one enormous single page** holding ~100 modules. Each module = H2 + Options table (Option/Default/Description) + Variables table + TOML example. Navigation is the right-hand "On this page" TOC + in-page anchors. At this length the right TOC is unusable and browser-find becomes the real interface.

**Preset gallery**: https://starship.rs/presets/ — screenshot cards, each image links to a per-preset page. Copy literally says *"To get details on how to use a preset, simply click on the image."* No filtering, no tags, no live preview, no one-click apply.

**Steal**: Nerd Font in the mono stack; presets-as-images-first; 13-locale i18n.
**Dated**: logo-only hero for a visual product; monolithic config page; unfiltered preset list; zero motion; visibly "default VitePress with a brand color swapped".

---

## 2. zed.dev

**Above the fold**: announcement bar (*"Early Access: DeltaDB, a new kind of version control"*), headline **"Your last next editor"**, subhead *"Zed is a minimal code editor crafted for speed and collaboration with humans and AI."*, CTAs **"Download now"** (primary) + **"Clone source"** (secondary, GitHub), microcopy *"Available for macOS, Linux, and Windows"*.

**Hero visual**: not a screenshot — a **simulated live product surface**. A recreated Zed chrome with a search field, a scrolling "recent activity" feed of branch names + diff stats + relative timestamps across three repos (`zed`, `cloud`, `zed.dev`), an agent transcript, and a code pane with **real inline diagnostics rendered as text** (`'couldHaveBeenAnEmail' is declared but its value is never read.`). It is DOM, not an image — selectable, crisp at any DPI, and it doubles as a "the project is alive" signal.

**Nav**: `Product` · `Resources` · `Extensions` · `Docs` · `Business` · `Pricing` · `Sign up` · `Download`.

**Below fold**: Fast / Agentic / Collaborative triad → testimonial wall (José Valim, Dan Abramov, Mike Bostock) → "Zed Just Works" video cards → feature card grid → extensions grid → founders' letter → blog.

**Visual language**: Tailwind + Next.js. Brand blue `#084ccf` / `#4482f8`; neutrals `#1b1e23`, `#dae4f8`, `#c6cad0`. **Typography is the differentiator**: self-hosted `IBM Plex Sans`, `IBM Plex Serif` (variable + italic), **`iA Writer Quattro S`** (the duospace face — very unusual on a dev site, gives editorial warmth) and **`Lilex`** for mono. Four families, deliberately.

**Docs**: https://zed.dev/docs/ is **mdBook output (elasticlunr search index) re-skinned inside the Next.js shell**. `S` keyboard shortcut for "Search docs…", light/dark toggle in the docs header. Settings reference is deliberately *not* a giant table — docs push you to the in-app Settings Editor ("search for any setting and change it directly", e.g. `buffer_font_family`). **Agent affordance**: `/docs/llms.txt` index plus Markdown versions of every docs page, advertised in-page.

**Steal**: DOM-rendered product hero; the llms.txt + `.md`-per-page pattern; four-family type system as brand.
**Dated**: nothing much; page weight is enormous (2.7 MB HTML).

---

## 3. bun.com

**Above the fold**: **"Bun is a fast JavaScript all-in-one toolkit"**; subhead *"Bun is a fast, incrementally adoptable all-in-one JavaScript, TypeScript & JSX toolkit."*

**Hero visual = the install command itself.** A copy box with a **Linux&macOS / Windows platform toggle**, a labelled primary button *"Install Bun v1.3.14"* (version in the button — always current, doubles as a release signal), and a secondary *"View install script"*. Immediately under: a customer logo bar (Lovable, CodeRabbit, Replit, Cursor) and a **benchmark bar chart with real numbers** ("Bundling 10,000 React components — Bun: 269.1ms").

**Nav**: `Build` · `Docs` · **`Reference`** · `Guides` · `Blog` · Discord · GitHub. The **three-way Docs / Reference / Guides split** is the important IA move.

**Below fold**: "Four tools, one toolkit" → benchmarks → "Who uses Bun?" (Claude Code, Railway, Midjourney) → comparison tables → API overview → framework interop → per-subcommand benchmark sections (`$ bun install`, `$ bun test`) → API carousel → testimonial carousel.

**Visual language** (from `/_assets/site-fe5bbc3c.css`): brand cream `#fbf0df`, `--black: #0b0a08`, `--pink: #ee81c3`, `--orange: #f89b4b`, `--blue: #00a6e1`, greys `#0d0e11`→`#f9fafb`, plus a bright accent ramp (`#ec4899 #a855f7 #60a5fa #34d399 #06b6d4`). `font-family: system-ui, sans-serif` — **no webfont for body**, mono via `--monospace-font`. Terminal chrome dots `#ff5f57 / #febc2e` appear as decoration.

**Reference**: https://bun.com/reference is **auto-generated from `packages/bun-types` TypeScript definitions**, with its own dedicated search field ("Search the reference…") and a module-tree sidebar, color-coded by type. **A separately-searchable, machine-generated reference portal, structurally distinct from hand-written docs.** Docs advertise `https://bun.com/docs/llms.txt` for agents.

**Steal**: install box *as* the hero with platform toggle and version-in-button; generated reference as its own searchable app; benchmarks with hard numbers above the fold.
**Dated**: system-ui body type reads generic; the homepage is extremely long.

---

## 4. biomejs.dev

**Above the fold**: **"One toolchain for your web project"** / *"Format, lint, and more in a fraction of a second."* CTAs **"Get started"** + **"View on GitHub"**. Hero visual = logo lockup only — same weakness as Starship.

**Nav**: `Docs` · `Enterprise` · `Playground` · `Blog` + theme/lang selectors + version switcher (v1.x / v2.x / next).

**Below fold**: Formatter with before/after code → Linter with a **real rendered diagnostic** (the terminal-style error block with source excerpt, caret, and suggestion — the strongest section) → unified `check` → 6 feature callouts → org logo grid (Astro, AWS, Cloudflare, Discord, Google, Microsoft, Vercel) → contributor avatars → sponsors.

**Doc tech**: **Astro v7.1.0 + Starlight v0.41.3** (confirmed via dual `<meta name="generator">`), **Pagefind** for search (fully static, no Algolia dependency).

**Visual language**: Starlight tokens overridden — `--sl-color-accent: #3d50f5` (light) / `#3369ff` (dark), `-high: #0f1c8a` / `#b3c7ff`, `-low: #cfd4fc` / `#131e4f`, greys `#23262f`/`#24272f`. Radii are conservative: `.25rem`, `.3rem`, `.5rem`, `8px`, `12px`. Syntax theme is **Night Owl** (`#403f53`, `#d6deeb`, `#c792ea`, `#7fdbca`, `#82aaff`, `#ecc48d`). Diagnostic colors `#b23834`/`#e2817f`/`#d9f5dd`/`#caece6`.

**Reference surface (511 rules)** — https://biomejs.dev/linter/javascript/rules/
- **Split by language first** (`/linter/javascript/rules`, `/css/rules`, `/json/rules`, `/graphql/rules`, `/html/rules`), then by **9 semantic groups** (a11y, complexity, correctness, nursery, performance, security, style, suspicious).
- Each group = a **table**: rule name (link) · one-line description · **badge column** (✓ recommended, 🔧 safe fix, ⚠️ unsafe fix, 🔮 next release), with a legend.
- A trailing **"Recommended rules"** section re-cuts the same set by severity — a *second view of the same data* for a different intent.
- **No client-side filtering.** Discovery is Pagefind + browser find.

**Steal**: two-axis split (language × group) before a flat list; badge column as scannable metadata; second re-cut view of the same catalog; Pagefind (zero-infra static search); the rendered-diagnostic hero block.
**Dated**: logo-only hero; a static table is straining at 511 rows.

---

## 5. astro.build

**Above the fold**: **"The web framework for content-driven websites"** / *"Astro powers the world's fastest marketing sites, blogs, e-commerce websites, and more."* CTA = **copyable `npm create astro@latest`** with "Copied!" feedback plus "Get Started". Hero background: abstract gradient.

**Nav**: `Documentation` · `Blog` · `Resources` (Themes, Integrations, Site showcase, Tutorials) · `Community` · `Enterprise` · GitHub.

**Below fold**: Server-First / Content-Driven / Customizable → **Core Web Vitals comparison chart** (66% vs 28–48%) → framework logo interop → 12 feature cards → theme ecosystem → partner agencies → sponsors → newsletter.

**Visual language**: Astro v7.1.3, Tailwind. `#6b7aab`, `#eef0f9`, `#2f3854`, `#17191e`, accents `#54b9ff` and mint `#4bf3c8`; framework brand colors (`#3178c6` TS, `#41b883` Vue, `#ff3e00` Svelte, `#61dafb` React) used as ecosystem signal.

**Theme gallery** — https://astro.build/themes/ — I rendered it in a browser: it is a **curated grid, not a faceted catalog**. Cards carry screenshot / title / description / author avatar+name / **Free|Paid pill**. The only real controls on the page are category *browse links* (Blog, E-commerce, Landing pages, Portfolio, Documentation) and a newsletter input — **no search input, no filter checkboxes, no sort control in the DOM**. Featured/sponsored themes occupy the top slots.

**Steal**: copy-command as CTA; measured comparison chart; card anatomy (thumb + title + desc + author + pill).
**Dated**: gallery has no in-page filtering despite hundreds of entries; sponsored-first ordering buries free/community work.

---

## 6. tauri.app

**Above the fold**: headline is just **"Tauri 2.0"**, subhead *"Create small, fast, secure, cross-platform applications"*. CTAs "Get started" + "Tauri 1.0 Documentation".

**Hero visual = a tabbed create-command widget** spanning 9 package managers/shells (Bash, PowerShell, Fish, npm, Yarn, pnpm, deno, bun, Cargo). Meets every user where they are, in one component.

**Nav**: `Guides` · `References` · `Blog` · `Releases` + socials. **Guides/References split at the top level** — same idiom as Bun.

**Doc tech**: **Astro v7.1.3 + Starlight v0.41.4**, search via **Meilisearch** with Pagefind also present, hosted on Netlify.

**Visual language**: `#21004b` deep purple, `#191919`, accents `#ff5caa`, `#ff4e62`, `#32e6e2`, `#05bdba`, `#ffc131`, `#24c8db`; Night Owl syntax again (`#403f53`, `#d6deeb`, `#82aaff`, `#ecc48d`).

**Large-surface handling** — https://tauri.app/plugin/ has the **best filtering primitive I found in this cohort**: official plugins as a **card grid with a platform filter dropdown** (All / Windows / Linux / macOS / iOS / Android) plus `Ctrl+K` search, backed by a **support matrix table** (plugin × 5 platforms with footnote markers). Community plugins are demoted to plain link lists. Reference splits into CLI / JavaScript API / config file.

**Steal**: multi-package-manager tabbed install widget; **facet dropdown over a card grid**; capability matrix table; official-vs-community tiering.
**Dated**: "Tauri 2.0" as the headline says nothing to a newcomer.

---

## 7. warp.dev

**Above the fold**: **"From the terminal to the cloud, with any agent"** / *"Warp is an open agentic development environment born from the terminal. Build your software factory with a flexible system designed to outlast whatever comes next."* CTAs **"Download Warp"** + **"Contact Sales"**.

Hero visual is a **configurator-style interactive panel** — pick model (OpenAI, Gemini), connectivity, inference provider (Bedrock, LiteLLM, OpenRouter).

**Nav** is a full enterprise mega-menu: `Products` (Warp Terminal / Warp Agent / Oz Agent Platform) · `Solutions` (Use Cases × Industry) · `Resources` (Docs, Blog, Community, Agent Kits, Events, Changelog, Roadmap, Support) · `Company` · `Enterprise` (Overview, Customers, Pricing).

**Below fold**: four tabbed product showcases → open-source announcement video → exec testimonial carousel (Microsoft, OpenAI, Stripe) → logo wall → "Start shipping with agents" → per-OS download.

**Visual language**: Next.js + **Sanity CMS** (`cdn.sanity.io` image pipeline). Near-black stack `#0b0b0b` / `#111111` / `#1f1f1f` / `#1c1a26` / `#373245`, lavender accents `#c7aeff` / `#bda6f7`, and a set of **tinted section washes** (`#1e142a`, `#141e30`, `#1a2a1a`, `#201a14`, `#1a1410`) used to color-code content zones on a dark ground. `Inter` throughout.

**Steal**: tinted-dark section washes for zoning; tabbed product showcase.
**Avoid**: the enterprise mega-menu and Solutions/Industry taxonomy are wrong for an OSS tool — Warp has visibly drifted from "terminal" to "agentic development environment", and the headline no longer says what you'd download.

---

## 8. ghostty.org

⚠️ **Caveat**: the homepage is Next.js App Router with a fully client-rendered `<main class="home-content-module__…homePage">` that **stayed empty** in my headless browser (no canvas, no video, no wasm in the resource log — only two font requests). WebFetch also returned title-only. So no verified hero copy.

What is verifiable:
- Body background `rgb(15, 15, 17)` = **`#0f0f11`, dark-only**; body font **`Pretendard Std Variable`** (self-hosted variable woff2) — a distinctive, non-Inter choice. Next.js + CSS Modules.
- Positioning line used across the site: *"Ghostty is a fast, feature-rich, and cross-platform terminal emulator that uses platform-native UI and GPU acceleration."*
- Nav: `Docs` · `Discord` · `GitHub` · `Download`.
- **Docs sidebar** (https://ghostty.org/docs): About Ghostty · Install · Configuration · Linux · Features · Terminal API (VT) · Help · Financial Support. Landing uses feature cards into each section.
- **Download page** is per-OS *sections* (macOS / Linux), version prominent ("Version 1.3.1"), links to release notes and to package-manager/build-from-source docs — **no inline copy-command**, which is weaker than Bun/Atuin.
- **Config reference** (https://ghostty.org/docs/config/reference): a **single page with hundreds of options**, ordered "roughly by how common they are… grouped with related options". Each entry: name heading, description, valid values, platform notes, **"Available since: 1.2.0"**, cross-references. The page explicitly tells you to *"utilize your browser's search functionality"* and admits *"In the future, we'll have a more user-friendly way to view and organize these options."*

**Steal**: per-option **"Available since: x.y.z"** version metadata; platform-scope notes per option; ordering by frequency-of-use rather than alphabetically; the Pretendard/`#0f0f11` dark-only restraint.
**Avoid**: a JS-only homepage that renders nothing without hydration (bad for crawlers, agents, and my own tooling); a config reference whose own maintainers call it unfit.

---

## 9. atuin.sh — **the most directly transferable site in this set**

**Above the fold**: **"Making your terminal magical"** / *"Sync, search, and back up your shell history with end-to-end encryption. Ask Atuin AI for help without leaving your prompt."*
- Dual CTA: a **copy-box with the install command** (`curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -LsSf https://setup.atuin.sh | sh` + "Copy") and a button styled as a shell command, **`$ get-started`**. The nav CTA is the same `$ get-started` token — the brand's button language *is* a prompt.
- Microcopy: *"Available for macOS, Linux, and Windows · bash, zsh, fish, and more"*.
- **Stat row**: `30K+ GitHub Stars` · `300+ Contributors` · `600M+ Synced Commands` — then a "Used by developers at" logo wall.

**Hero visual — the key finding.** Atuin ships a hand-built **`demo-term/demo-term.css` + `demo-term.js`**: an animated terminal **rendered in DOM, not a screenshot or asciinema cast**. Its content is literally a prompt line —

> `~/src/api  on main  via 🦀 v1.92  ❯` … `ctrl` `+` `r` … `<tab> edit · <enter> run · synced 78,594`

…followed by animated history rows with duration/recency columns (`git pull --rebase 2s 8h ago`, `kubectl rollout status deploy/api 12s now`). **A competitor is already rendering an Oh-My-Posh/Starship-style prompt in HTML on their homepage.**

**Nav**: `History` · `AI` · `Blog` · `Docs` · GitHub · `$ get-started`. Feature sections use numbered `01/02/03` eyebrows.

**Visual language**: `--bg-deep: #0f1722`, greens `#38c85a` / `#a8ecba` / `#d4f5de`, text ramp `#e8f0e9` / `#8fa1a8` / `#5a6870`, warm secondary `#f2d08a` / `#f0e8d3` / `#c4d86f` / `#d8d0bc`, terminal ANSI accents `#ffb86c` `#f06d5f` `#97c4bd`. Fonts: **`DM Sans`** body + **`Space Mono`** mono — both non-default, both cheap, and the pairing does more brand work than Starship's Inter.

**Doc tech**: hand-rolled static HTML, very light. Docs on a subdomain.

**Steal**: essentially everything — DOM-rendered animated terminal hero, prompt-as-button-language, copy-box + stats + logo wall stack, numbered feature eyebrows, self-host escape hatch inline (*"Prefer your own infra? The sync server is open source — self-host it."*).

---

## 10. charm.land (charm.sh 301s here)

**Above the fold**: **"We make the command line glamorous."** Featured product slot: **Crush** — *"Your new coding bestie, now available in your favourite terminal."*, CTA **"Get Crush"**, microcopy *"Available now for macOS, Linux, Windows, and BSD."* Hero visual is mascot illustration.

**Nav**: `Home` · `Libs` · `Apps` · `Enterprise` · `Blog` + 7 socials. Note: **the catalog is split into Libs vs Apps** — the only navigation the site needs.

**Product catalog** ("Build with Charm — Everything you need to build great stuff for the terminal. Always open-source."): an **8-card grid** — Bubble Tea, Huh, Lip Gloss, Wish, Glamour, Bubbles, Log, Harmonica. Each card = **mascot illustration + name + a two-word flavor/attribute pair + one-line description + GitHub link**. The flavor pairs are the trick: *"Flavor: Taro"*, *"Glossiness: Very"*, *"Type: Tapioca"*, *"Hot: Totally"* — pure personality occupying the slot where a boring metadata chip would sit.

Then **"More stuff"**: 4 large feature cards (Mods, gum, Glow, Skate) with per-product CTAs in-voice — *"Chew Gum"*, *"Get Glow"*, *"Let's Roll"*.

Social proof is one line, no logo wall: *"Industrial grade. Charm technology lives in over 25,000 applications."* Footer signs off `vt100@charm.land` / `haters > /dev/null™`.

**Visual language**: cream ground `#fffdf5` / `#fffaf1` (**light-first — the outlier in this cohort**), pink/purple applied via illustration rather than CSS tokens; heavy custom mascot art.

**Steal**: card metadata slot repurposed for voice; per-product CTA copy; two-bucket catalog split; one-line credibility instead of a logo wall.
**Avoid**: illustration-heavy identity is expensive and doesn't survive a maintainer handoff; near-zero product screenshots for products whose whole point is how they look.

---

## 11. Astral: uv + ruff (Material for MkDocs)

**uv** (https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) — **no marketing site at all**; the docs *are* the homepage. Headline *"An extremely fast Python package and project manager, written in Rust"*, hero = **benchmark bar charts** (Trio dependency resolution), install commands split macOS/Linux vs Windows.
Sidebar: `Introduction` · `Getting started` · `Guides` · `Concepts` · `Reference`, with Integrations (Docker, Jupyter, GitHub Actions, AWS Lambda), Authentication, Troubleshooting nested. **Reference is flat**: Commands / Settings / Environment variables / Storage as sibling generated pages. Search sits at the top of the nav (Material's standard). Footer credits **Material for MkDocs**.

**ruff** (https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/) — same stack. Landing = logo, benchmark bar chart, bullets, developer testimonials, playground link.
**Reference surface (900+ rules)** at `/rules/`: **grouped by originating linter/plugin — ~50 sections** (flake8-bugbear (B), isort (I), Pylint (PL) with Convention/Error/Refactor/Warning sub-splits, Ruff-specific (RUF)…), each a table with **Code · Name · Message · Status** where status carries stable/preview/deprecated/removed **and** "🛠️ Automatic fix available". Navigation = a TOC of the ~50 groups + anchors. **No client-side filtering.** Separate `/settings/` reference and a `/rules/#default-rules` cut.

**Steal**: grouping the reference by *provenance* (which upstream it came from) — for Oh My Posh the analogue is grouping segments by domain; the stable/preview/deprecated lifecycle badge; docs-as-homepage when the audience is 100% technical.
**Dated**: Material for MkDocs is instantly recognizable and carries zero brand; 900 rows across 50 tables with no filter is the same wall Starship and Ghostty hit.

## 11b. mise.jdx.dev

Headline **"Your dev environment, prepped and ready"** / *"One tool that manages dev tools, env vars, and tasks per project."*, CTAs "Getting Started" + "Demo", hero includes a live `mise.toml` example with `[tools]` / `[env]` / `[tasks.test]`. VitePress (`#VPContent`).

**Registry of 1000+ tools** (https://mise.jdx.dev/registry.html) is a **plain static three-column table** (Short · Full · OS) with **no search box**. mise explicitly **offloads discovery to the CLI**: *"`mise registry` can be used to list all tools… `mise use` without any arguments will show a `tui` to select a tool to install."* That is a legitimate architectural answer (the TUI is the filter) but it means the *web* catalog is close to useless for browsing — and it's the exact failure mode to avoid if the website is meant to be a discovery surface.

---

## 12. Baseline: ohmyposh.dev today

- **Docusaurus v3.10.2**, Algolia DocSearch, Inter loaded from `rsms.me/inter/inter.css`, ~19 KB HTML.
- Homepage: *"The most customizable and fastest prompt engine for any shell"*, CTAs **"Get Started →"** + **"See themes →"**, static hero image. Nav: Docs · Blog · Sponsor · Swag + GitHub/Discord/Bluesky.
- Segment pages (e.g. `/docs/segments/cli/argocd`) follow a rigid template: **What** → **Sample Configuration** (JSON/YAML/TOML tabs) → **Template** → **Properties** table (Name/Type/Description). Sidebar groups segments by CLI / Cloud / Health / Languages / Music / Source control / System / Web, alphabetical within.
- **Segment pages contain no visual preview whatsoever** — for a product that renders pixels, every reference page is text-only.
- Themes gallery (`/docs/themes`): ~150+ entries, **alphabetical list of name + PNG screenshot**, links to the GitHub raw file, **no search, no filter, no tags, no live preview, no one-click apply**, and it defers to GitHub for the current list.
- Install docs use per-shell tabs; heavy emoji in sidebar labels (`💡 Getting Started > ✨ Prompt`).

Relative to this cohort the gaps are: no hero demo, no theme filtering/preview, no visual on reference pages, no llms.txt/agent affordance, and an unmodified-Docusaurus visual identity.

---

# Synthesis

## A. The 3–4 dominant idioms in 2026

**1. The hero *is* the install command, and the version number lives in the button.**
Bun (`Install Bun v1.3.14` + Linux/macOS↔Windows toggle), Atuin (copy-box + `$ get-started`), Astro (`npm create astro@latest`, "Copied!"), Tauri (9-way package-manager tabs), Starship (install block inlined on the homepage). Nobody makes you click through to a getting-started page to see the command. Corollary: **Ghostty's download page, which offers no copy-command, is the outlier and it reads as friction.**

**2. Product surfaces are re-rendered in the DOM, not screenshotted.**
Zed's activity feed + code pane with real inline diagnostics; Atuin's `demo-term`; Biome's rendered diagnostic block; Warp's interactive configurator; Bun's syntax-highlighted API carousel. Benefits: crisp at every DPI, selectable/copyable, themeable, dark/light-reactive, diffable in git, and localizable. **PNG screenshots now read as dated** — which is precisely what Starship's presets page and Oh My Posh's theme gallery both are.

**3. Dark-first, but with *zoned* dark rather than one flat black.**
Ghostty `#0f0f11` dark-only; ray.so `#0d0d0d`; Warp stacks `#0b0b0b`/`#111111`/`#1f1f1f` and then adds **tinted section washes** (`#1e142a` purple, `#141e30` blue, `#1a2a1a` green, `#201a14` amber) to color-code content zones; Atuin `#0f1722` with a green/warm-cream dual accent. The 2026 refinement over 2023 is calibrated multi-step neutral ramps plus one saturated accent — **not** gradient-mesh, not glassmorphism, not noise/grain (I found essentially none of those in this cohort). Motion is minimal and confined to hero and section transitions.

**4. Typography is now the brand.**
Zed runs four self-hosted families (IBM Plex Sans, IBM Plex Serif, iA Writer Quattro S, Lilex). Ghostty picked Pretendard Variable. Atuin picked DM Sans + Space Mono. Bun deliberately uses `system-ui`. The tools that read as "default template" are exactly the ones on stock Inter over a stock generator theme — **Starship and Oh My Posh both sit in that bucket.** For a prompt engine specifically: **Starship prepends `"Nerd Font"` to its mono stack** so glyphs render in code blocks; that is a one-line, high-leverage steal.

**Emerging fifth idiom — the agent affordance.** Bun (`/docs/llms.txt`), Zed (`/docs/llms.txt` **plus a `.md` version of every page**, advertised in-page). This is becoming table stakes and is cheap on any generator.

## B. Navigating a large reference surface — what actually works

Observed strategies, ranked by how well they hold up:

| Strategy | Who | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **Split the reference by axis before listing** (language × category) | Biome: 5 language pages × 9 groups | **Best.** No single page exceeds ~80 rows. |
| **Facet dropdown over a card grid** | Tauri plugins (platform filter + `Ctrl+K`) | **Best-in-cohort interaction.** Only site that filters in the browser. |
| **Group by provenance/domain, table per group** | Ruff (~50 linter groups), Biome | Scales to ~900 rows but is scroll-and-find, not filter. |
| **Generated reference as its own searchable app** | Bun `/reference` (from TS types, own search field) | **Strong** — separates hand-written prose from machine truth, and never drifts. |
| **Second re-cut of the same catalog** | Biome "Recommended rules" by severity; Ruff "Default rules" | Cheap, high value — serves a different intent from the same data. |
| **Capability matrix table** | Tauri plugin × 5 platforms | Excellent for cross-cutting support questions. |
| Single giant page + right-hand TOC | Starship `/config/` (~100 modules) | **Breaks.** TOC is unusable at this length. |
| Single giant page + "use browser find" | Ghostty config reference | **Breaks, and maintainers say so in the page.** |
| Static table, discovery offloaded to CLI/TUI | mise registry (1000+ tools) | Defensible for a CLI, **fails as a web discovery surface.** |

**The pattern that keeps recurring in the ones that work**: metadata rendered as a **badge column** rather than prose — Biome (✓ recommended / 🔧 safe fix / ⚠️ unsafe fix / 🔮 next release, with a legend), Ruff (stable/preview/deprecated/removed + 🛠️ auto-fix), Ghostty (**"Available since: 1.2.0"** and platform-scope notes per option). Badges are scannable, filterable if you later add JS, and answer "can I use this yet?" without opening the page.

**Ordering**: Ghostty orders options **by frequency of use and semantic grouping, not alphabetically**. Oh My Posh's segment sidebar is alphabetical-within-category; frequency ordering (or a "most used" cluster) would surface `git`, `path`, `python`, `node` above `argocd`.

## C. Theme gallery / showcase patterns

**The reference implementation is ray.so/themes** (Raycast's Theme Explorer, open source at `raycast/ray-so`). Verified in-browser:
- **Live-rendered preview, not a screenshot** — the actual app chrome ("Search for apps and commands…", list rows, primary text) rendered in the theme's own colors, in DOM.
- **Dark / Light segmented toggle** at gallery level, each linking to a representative theme (`/chris/almost-cyan`, `/luxonauta/alucard`).
- **URL is `/{author}/{theme-slug}`** — every theme is individually addressable and shareable; theme state is encoded in the URL.
- **One-click "Add to Raycast"** deep-link — zero copy-paste between browse and apply. This is the single biggest conversion lever and nothing in the Oh My Posh cohort has it.
- Authoring loop closed: Theme Studio → right-click → *Copy as URL* (produces a gallery link) or *Copy as JSON*. **The gallery is the sharing format.**
- Dark `#0d0d0d`, Inter, Radix-style grey scales (`gray-2`…`gray-12`, `gray-a4`…`gray-a11`), pill/`rounded-md` radii.

Supporting patterns:
- **Card anatomy** (Astro themes, Vercel templates): thumbnail · title · 1–2 line description · **author avatar + name** · status pill. Authorship is what makes a community gallery feel like a community.
- **Faceted sidebar with per-facet counts and a global "Clear"**, URL-driven so filter state is shareable/bookmarkable — Vercel `/templates` is the model (Use Case / Framework / CSS / Database / Auth / CMS, each with a selected-count indicator).
- **Tiering**: Tauri's official-cards-vs-community-links, Astro's featured/sponsor row. Useful, but see anti-patterns.
- **Screenshot cards linking to per-item pages** — Starship presets. Minimum viable; what Oh My Posh has today, minus even the per-item page.

**Concrete implication for an Oh My Posh theme gallery**: render prompts as HTML/CSS from the theme JSON (segments, colors, powerline separators, Nerd Font glyphs) instead of committing 150 PNGs; give each theme `/themes/{name}`; facet by *needs Nerd Font · has powerline · segment count · light/dark · segments used*; add a one-click apply (copy `oh-my-posh init pwsh --config <url>` or a deep link); and let the same renderer power previews on segment reference pages.

## D. Anti-patterns to avoid

1. **Logo-only hero for a visual product.** Starship and Biome both lead with a logo. If the product's value is what appears on screen, the hero must show it. Atuin, Zed, and Bun all do.
2. **Screenshot galleries.** 150 PNGs are stale on merge, unfilterable, un-themeable, invisible to search, and heavy. Render from source data.
3. **The monolithic reference page.** Starship's `/config/` and Ghostty's config reference are the two clearest failures in this study — and Ghostty's own docs concede it.
4. **Catalogs with no in-browser filter.** Ruff (900 rules), Biome (511), mise (1000 tools), Astro themes (hundreds) — all rely on browser find or an external search. Tauri's platform dropdown is the lone counterexample and it's trivially cheap.
5. **A JS-only homepage.** ghostty.org served me an empty `<main>` with a browser attached. Whatever agents, crawlers, and link previews see, that's what they see too. Anything above the fold should be in the HTML.
6. **Enterprise mega-menu drift.** Warp's `Solutions › Industry › Insurance` taxonomy on what people still install as a terminal. For an OSS tool, a 4–6 item nav (Atuin: History · AI · Blog · Docs; Ghostty: Docs · Discord · GitHub · Download) is correct.
7. **Sponsored-first gallery ordering.** Astro's themes page is 12+ "Paid" cards deep before community work appears. Corrosive to an OSS community gallery.
8. **Version-number headlines.** "Tauri 2.0" tells a first-time visitor nothing. Put the version in the install button (Bun) instead.
9. **Un-themed default generators.** Stock VitePress with one swapped brand color (Starship), stock Material for MkDocs (uv, ruff), stock Docusaurus (Oh My Posh). Instantly legible as "we didn't design this." The cheapest fix with the largest return is **type + a calibrated neutral ramp**, not illustration.
10. **Emoji as sidebar taxonomy.** Oh My Posh's `💡 Getting Started` / `✨ Prompt` doesn't survive translation, search indexing, or scanning at density.

## Reference URLs

<title>Oh My Posh — website design & IA proposal</title>

<style>
/* ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   Document shell tokens
   Neutral ramp carries a slight blue-slate bias, borrowed from
   the product's own rose-pine/terminal ground rather than a
   pure grey.
   ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
:root {
  --ink:        #131820;
  --ink-2:      #3d4757;
  --ink-3:      #6b7788;
  --ground:     #f7f8fa;
  --panel:      #ffffff;
  --rule:       #dde2ea;
  --rule-soft:  #e9edf3;
  --accent:     #1f6fd0;
  --accent-ink: #0f4c96;
  --accent-wash:#e8f0fb;
  --amber:      #a86b12;
  --amber-wash: #fdf3e0;
  --good:       #1a7f52;
  --bad:        #b4453a;

  --mono: ui-monospace, "SF Mono", "Cascadia Mono", "Cascadia Code", "JetBrains Mono", Menlo, Consolas, monospace;
  --sans: system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", Roboto, "Helvetica Neue", sans-serif;

  --measure: 68ch;
  --pad: clamp(1.25rem, 4vw, 3rem);
}

@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root {
    --ink:        #e3e9f2;
    --ink-2:      #a5b1c2;
    --ink-3:      #77footer;
    --ink-3:      #7b8798;
    --ground:     #0e1117;
    --panel:      #151a22;
    --rule:       #262e3a;
    --rule-soft:  #1d242e;
    --accent:     #63a4f0;
    --accent-ink: #a8caf7;
    --accent-wash:#15243a;
    --amber:      #e0ac5a;
    --amber-wash: #2a2115;
    --good:       #4fbf8b;
    --bad:        #e07a6e;
  }
}

:root[data-theme="dark"] {
  --ink:        #e3e9f2;
  --ink-2:      #a5b1c2;
  --ink-3:      #7b8798;
  --ground:     #0e1117;
  --panel:      #151a22;
  --rule:       #262e3a;
  --rule-soft:  #1d242e;
  --accent:     #63a4f0;
  --accent-ink: #a8caf7;
  --accent-wash:#15243a;
  --amber:      #e0ac5a;
  --amber-wash: #2a2115;
  --good:       #4fbf8b;
  --bad:        #e07a6e;
}

:root[data-theme="light"] {
  --ink:        #131820;
  --ink-2:      #3d4757;
  --ink-3:      #6b7788;
  --ground:     #f7f8fa;
  --panel:      #ffffff;
  --rule:       #dde2ea;
  --rule-soft:  #e9edf3;
  --accent:     #1f6fd0;
  --accent-ink: #0f4c96;
  --accent-wash:#e8f0fb;
  --amber:      #a86b12;
  --amber-wash: #fdf3e0;
  --good:       #1a7f52;
  --bad:        #b4453a;
}

/* ── base ───────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.doc {
  background: var(--ground);
  color: var(--ink);
  font-family: var(--sans);
  font-size: 16px;
  line-height: 1.6;
  -webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;
}
.doc *,
.doc *::before,
.doc *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }

.wrap {
  max-width: 1120px;
  margin: 0 auto;
  padding: 0 var(--pad);
}

.doc h1, .doc h2, .doc h3, .doc h4 {
  text-wrap: balance;
  letter-spacing: -0.018em;
  line-height: 1.15;
  margin: 0;
  font-weight: 640;
}

.doc p { margin: 0; max-width: var(--measure); }
.doc a { color: var(--accent); text-decoration-thickness: 1px; text-underline-offset: 2px; }
.doc a:focus-visible,
.doc button:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid var(--accent); outline-offset: 3px; border-radius: 3px; }

/* Eyebrow — monospace is the subject's own vernacular, used only
   as a structural marker, never as body text. */
.eyebrow {
  font-family: var(--mono);
  font-size: 0.68rem;
  letter-spacing: 0.16em;
  text-transform: uppercase;
  color: var(--ink-3);
  margin: 0;
}

.stack   { display: flex; flex-direction: column; }
.gap-2   { gap: 0.5rem; }
.gap-3   { gap: 0.75rem; }
.gap-4   { gap: 1rem; }
.gap-6   { gap: 1.5rem; }
.gap-8   { gap: 2rem; }

section.band { padding: clamp(2.75rem, 6vw, 4.5rem) 0; border-top: 1px solid var(--rule-soft); }
section.band:first-of-type { border-top: 0; }

.lede { font-size: 1.075rem; color: var(--ink-2); }
.small { font-size: 0.875rem; color: var(--ink-2); }
.tiny { font-size: 0.8rem; color: var(--ink-3); }

/* ── masthead ───────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.masthead {
  padding: clamp(3rem, 8vw, 5.5rem) 0 clamp(2rem, 4vw, 3rem);
  border-bottom: 1px solid var(--rule);
}
.masthead h1 {
  font-size: clamp(2rem, 5.2vw, 3.1rem);
  max-width: 20ch;
}
.masthead .lede { max-width: 60ch; font-size: 1.15rem; }

.meta-row {
  display: flex;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
  gap: 0.5rem 1.75rem;
  font-family: var(--mono);
  font-size: 0.75rem;
  color: var(--ink-3);
  border-top: 1px solid var(--rule-soft);
  padding-top: 1rem;
}
.meta-row b { color: var(--ink-2); font-weight: 500; }

/* ── findings ───────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.stat-grid {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(160px, 1fr));
  gap: 1px;
  background: var(--rule);
  border: 1px solid var(--rule);
  border-radius: 8px;
  overflow: hidden;
}
.stat {
  background: var(--panel);
  padding: 1.1rem 1.15rem;
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
  gap: 0.3rem;
}
.stat .n {
  font-family: var(--mono);
  font-size: 1.6rem;
  font-weight: 600;
  font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums;
  letter-spacing: -0.03em;
  color: var(--ink);
}
.stat .n.warn { color: var(--bad); }
.stat .l { font-size: 0.8rem; color: var(--ink-3); line-height: 1.35; }

.findings { display: grid; gap: 1px; background: var(--rule); border: 1px solid var(--rule); border-radius: 8px; overflow: hidden; }
.finding {
  background: var(--panel);
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 7.5rem 1fr;
  gap: 0 1.25rem;
  padding: 0.95rem 1.15rem;
  align-items: baseline;
}
.finding .sev {
  font-family: var(--mono);
  font-size: 0.66rem;
  letter-spacing: 0.1em;
  text-transform: uppercase;
  padding: 0.15rem 0.45rem;
  border-radius: 3px;
  justify-self: start;
  white-space: nowrap;
}
.sev.block { background: var(--bad); color: #fff; }
.sev.friction { background: var(--amber-wash); color: var(--amber); border: 1px solid currentColor; }
.sev.polish { background: var(--rule-soft); color: var(--ink-3); }
.finding p { font-size: 0.92rem; }
.finding code { font-family: var(--mono); font-size: 0.86em; background: var(--rule-soft); padding: 0.08em 0.32em; border-radius: 3px; }
@media (max-width: 620px) {
  .finding { grid-template-columns: 1fr; gap: 0.45rem; }
}

/* ── tables ─────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.tbl-scroll { overflow-x: auto; border: 1px solid var(--rule); border-radius: 8px; background: var(--panel); }
table.t { border-collapse: collapse; width: 100%; font-size: 0.88rem; min-width: 640px; }
table.t th, table.t td { text-align: left; padding: 0.7rem 0.9rem; border-bottom: 1px solid var(--rule-soft); vertical-align: top; }
table.t thead th {
  font-family: var(--mono);
  font-size: 0.68rem;
  letter-spacing: 0.11em;
  text-transform: uppercase;
  color: var(--ink-3);
  font-weight: 500;
  background: var(--rule-soft);
  border-bottom: 1px solid var(--rule);
}
table.t tbody tr:last-child td { border-bottom: 0; }
table.t td:first-child { font-weight: 560; color: var(--ink); white-space: nowrap; }
.verdict { font-family: var(--mono); font-size: 0.74rem; white-space: nowrap; }
.verdict.up { color: var(--good); }
.verdict.down { color: var(--bad); }

/* ── IA trees ───────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.ia-grid { display: grid; gap: 1.25rem; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(310px, 1fr)); align-items: start; }
.ia {
  background: var(--panel);
  border: 1px solid var(--rule);
  border-radius: 10px;
  overflow: hidden;
}
.ia > header { padding: 1rem 1.15rem 0.85rem; border-bottom: 1px solid var(--rule-soft); display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 0.35rem; }
.ia > header h3 { font-size: 1.02rem; }
.ia .tree {
  font-family: var(--mono);
  font-size: 0.78rem;
  line-height: 1.75;
  padding: 0.9rem 1.15rem 1.15rem;
  margin: 0;
  white-space: pre;
  overflow-x: auto;
  color: var(--ink-2);
}
.ia .tree b { color: var(--ink); font-weight: 600; }
.ia .tree i { color: var(--good); font-style: normal; }
.ia .tree s { color: var(--ink-3); }
.ia footer { padding: 0.85rem 1.15rem 1.05rem; border-top: 1px solid var(--rule-soft); font-size: 0.85rem; color: var(--ink-2); }

/* ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   MOCKUPS
   Each mockup is its own visual world with its own tokens.
   They deliberately ignore the document theme — they are
   artwork samples, not page chrome.
   ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.mock-frame {
  border: 1px solid var(--rule);
  border-radius: 12px;
  overflow: hidden;
  box-shadow: 0 1px 2px rgba(10, 16, 26, 0.06), 0 12px 32px -20px rgba(10, 16, 26, 0.35);
}
.mock-caption {
  display: flex;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
  gap: 0.4rem 1rem;
  align-items: baseline;
  font-family: var(--mono);
  font-size: 0.7rem;
  letter-spacing: 0.08em;
  text-transform: uppercase;
  color: var(--ink-3);
  padding: 0.6rem 0.15rem 0;
}

.mock { font-size: 15px; line-height: 1.5; }
.mock * { box-sizing: border-box; }
.mock .m-wrap { max-width: 980px; margin: 0 auto; padding: 0 1.75rem; }
.mock .m-nav {
  display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 1.35rem;
  padding: 0.85rem 1.75rem;
  font-size: 0.82rem;
}
.mock .m-nav .brand { font-weight: 700; letter-spacing: -0.01em; }
.mock .m-nav .spacer { margin-left: auto; }
.mock h2.m-h { font-size: clamp(1.6rem, 3.6vw, 2.5rem); letter-spacing: -0.028em; line-height: 1.08; margin: 0; text-wrap: balance; }
.mock p.m-sub { margin: 0; font-size: 0.95rem; max-width: 52ch; }
.mock .m-row { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 0.7rem; align-items: center; }
.mock .m-btn {

<section class="band">
  <div class="wrap stack gap-8">
    <div class="stack gap-3">
      <p class="eyebrow">01 — Where we are</p>
      <h2 style="font-size:1.65rem;">The homepage is still the 2020 Docusaurus scaffold</h2>
      <p class="lede">
        Two buttons, three emoji paragraphs, one static PNG — about 130 lines total. Everything that would
        make a visitor install has to be found somewhere else.
      </p>
    </div>

    <div class="stat-grid">
      <div class="stat"><span class="n">130</span><span class="l">lines in the entire homepage</span></div>
      <div class="stat"><span class="n">11</span><span class="l">top-level sidebar entries, all emoji-prefixed</span></div>
      <div class="stat"><span class="n warn">28,093<span style="font-size:0.6em">px</span></span><span class="l">height of the themes page — 124 PNGs, 8 MB, no filter</span></div>
      <div class="stat"><span class="n warn">0</span><span class="l">segment reference pages showing what the segment looks like</span></div>
      <div class="stat"><span class="n">117</span><span class="l">segments, reachable only by guessing a category</span></div>
      <div class="stat"><span class="n warn">3</span><span class="l">clicks minimum from homepage to an install command</span></div>
    </div>

    <div class="stack gap-4">
      <h3 style="font-size:1.05rem;">Concrete defects found in the codebase</h3>
      <div class="findings">
        <div class="finding">
          <span class="sev block">Blocking</span>
          <p><b>“Get Started →” lands on a theory page.</b> <code>configuration/introduction.mdx</code> carries <code>slug: /</code>, so the primary homepage CTA opens an essay about blocks and segments — not an install command. The sidebar’s actual first item is Getting Started › Installation › Windows, which the CTA never reaches.</p>
        </div>
        <div class="finding">
          <span class="sev block">Blocking</span>
          <p><b>No index pages exist.</b> Getting Started, Segments, and all eight segment sub-groups are bare categories — clicking them only expands a tree. <code>static/llms.txt</code> already links <code>/docs/segments/overview</code> and <code>/docs/configuration/overview</code>; neither page exists, and <code>onBrokenLinks: 'ignore'</code> hides it.</p>
        </div>
        <div class="finding">
          <span class="sev block">Blocking</span>
          <p><b>Segment discovery depends on guessing a bucket.</b> <code>kubectl</code>, <code>helm</code> and <code>argocd</code> live under CLI, not Cloud. <code>docker</code> is CLI. <code>winget</code> is System. Every group is <code>collapsed: true</code> by default, so the default view of 117 segments shows nothing.</p>
        </div>
        <div class="finding">
          <span class="sev friction">Friction</span>
          <p><b>The theme gallery is one 124-image scroll.</b> No search, no tags, no filter, no per-theme URL, no way to apply one. The Nerd-Font requirement is a sentence of prose, not a facet. It is also one of only two homepage CTAs.</p>
        </div>
        <div class="finding">
          <span class="sev friction">Friction</span>
          <p><b>The FAQ absorbs everything with no home.</b> 24 headings covering PowerShell, fonts, Windows Terminal, JetBrains, Conda, venv, Zsh, Fish, Xonsh, Vim and posh-git. There is no troubleshooting section, no per-shell page and no per-terminal page.</p>
        </div>
        <div class="finding">
          <span class="sev friction">Friction</span>
          <p><b>Orphan and near-orphan docs.</b> <code>docs/auth.mdx</code> is in no sidebar — only reachable via an OAuth redirect. <code>Advanced</code> is a category with exactly one child. <code>dsc</code>, <code>themes</code>, <code>share</code>, <code>faq</code>, <code>migrating</code> and <code>contributors</code> float loose at root.</p>
        </div>
        <div class="finding">
          <span class="sev friction">Friction</span>
          <p><b>Navbar priorities are inverted.</b> Sponsor and Swag sit in primary left nav beside Docs and Blog, above a non-closeable sponsor bar. The blog has averaged under one post a year since 2022. Themes and Segments — the two things people actually come for — are not in the nav at all.</p>
        </div>
        <div class="finding">
          <span class="sev polish">Polish</span>
          <p><b>The CSS has hash-coupled selectors.</b> <code>a.getStarted_Sjon</code> and <code>.themedImage_ToTc</code> target generated CSS-module hashes and break silently on upgrade. <code>--ifm-color-primary-lightest</code> is <code>rgb(8,9,10)</code> — near-black. <code>--ifm-font-family-monospace</code> is set to <code>"Inter"</code>. Fira Code is fetched from Google Fonts and never referenced.</p>
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

            <td style="text-align:right;"><span class="verdict down">avoid</span></td>

          <tr>
            <td>docs.astral.sh</td>
            <td>Docs <em>are</em> the homepage. Benchmark charts above the fold.</td>
            <td>Material sidebar.</td>
            <td>900 rules in ~50 tables, lifecycle badges, no filter.</td>
            <td style="text-align:right;"><span class="verdict up">badge column</span></td>
          </tr>
          <tr>
            <td>warp.dev</td>
            <td>Interactive configurator panel.</td>
            <td>Enterprise mega-menu.</td>
            <td>—</td>
            <td style="text-align:right;"><span class="verdict down">nav drift</span></td>

        </tbody>
      </table>
    </div>

    <div class="stack gap-4">
      <h3 style="font-size:1.05rem;">The four idioms</h3>
      <div class="findings">
        <div class="finding"><span class="sev polish">Idiom 1</span><p><b>The hero is the install command.</b> Bun, Atuin, Astro and Tauri all put a copyable command above the fold, with an OS or package-manager toggle and the current version in the button. Nobody makes you click through.</p></div>
        <div class="finding"><span class="sev polish">Idiom 2</span><p><b>Product surfaces are rendered in the DOM, never screenshotted.</b> Crisp at any DPI, selectable, theme-reactive, diffable in git, indexable. PNG galleries now read as dated — which is exactly what our themes page is.</p></div>
        <div class="finding"><span class="sev polish">Idiom 3</span><p><b>Dark-first, but zoned.</b> One flat black is out. Warp tints section washes purple/blue/green/amber over a near-black ground; Atuin runs <code>#0f1722</code> with a green and warm-cream pair. Calibrated neutral ramps plus one saturated accent — no gradient mesh, no glass, no grain.</p></div>
        <div class="finding"><span class="sev polish">Idiom 4</span><p><b>Typography carries the brand.</b> Zed self-hosts four families; Ghostty picked Pretendard; Atuin pairs DM Sans with Space Mono. The sites that read as templates are the ones on stock Inter over a stock generator theme — Starship and Oh My Posh, both.</p></div>
      </div>
      <div class="callout">
        <b>Free win, one line:</b> Starship prepends <code>"Nerd Font"</code> to its monospace stack, so Nerd Font glyphs render correctly in code blocks for anyone who has the font installed. Every powerline character in our docs currently falls back to tofu for visitors without it.
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

Mockups are DOM — powerline chevrons cut with `clip-path`, no images. That itself is the argument.

## Core finding

Site sells a thing whose whole value is pixels on screen. Shows almost none of them. Starship has same disease (logo-only hero). Atuin, Zed, Bun all render product surfaces in DOM now — screenshots read as dated.

**Hard defects, not opinions:**
- `configuration/introduction.mdx` has `slug: /` — "Get Started →" lands on block/segment theory, not an install command. 3 clicks to a command.
- Zero index pages. `static/llms.txt` already links `/docs/segments/overview` + `/docs/configuration/overview`; neither exists. `onBrokenLinks: 'ignore'` hides it.
- Themes page: 28,093px, 124 PNGs, 8MB, no filter/tags/per-theme URL/apply.
- 117 segments, all groups `collapsed: true`, discovery = guess the bucket (`kubectl`/`helm`/`argocd` are CLI, not Cloud).
- `custom.css` targets generated hashes (`a.getStarted_Sjon`, `.themedImage_ToTc`). `--ifm-font-family-monospace: "Inter"`. `--ifm-color-primary-lightest: rgb(8,9,10)`. Fira Code fetched, never used.
- `auth.mdx` orphaned — no sidebar entry, reachable only via OAuth redirect.

## Three directions

| | A · Calibrated | B · Terminal Native | C · Studio |
|---|---|---|---|
| Effort | days | weeks | a quarter |
| IA | IA-1 Tidy | IA-2 Four doors | IA-3 Studio-first |
| Kills PNG gallery | no | yes | yes, editable |

**Recommend B + IA-2, built so C stays reachable.** Load-bearing piece in both is one prompt renderer: `config + mock context → DOM`. `segment_data.json` is already a complete fixture. `export_themes.mjs` already knows author + bg per theme. Build renderer once behind a stable interface; B uses it at build time, C later drives it from an editor.

IA-2 moves Themes and Segments *out* of `/docs` into faceted first-class sections, splits Configure prose from a generated Reference tier (Bun's move), and gives Sponsor/Swag/Blog an honest home in Community instead of primary nav.

## Open decisions that change the plan

1. Stay on Docusaurus, or move to Astro + Starlight (Biome, Tauri)? C is materially cheaper on Astro.
2. JS renderer (drift risk vs Go engine) or compile engine to WASM (one truth, heavier)?
3. Nerd Font subset served from site — otherwise live previews are tofu. Licensing + weight.
4. Blog: 6 posts since 2022. Fold into Community with release notes, or retire.

Phase 0 in the artifact is all bug fixes, no design calls — shippable immediately, independent of which direction you pick. Say the word and I'll plan it.

content.text:
Today it comes from the Go binary. Nothing on the web renders anything.

## Current pipeline

[export_themes.mjs](website/export_themes.mjs) is a shell-out loop:

```
themes/*.omp.json
  → oh-my-posh config export image --config X --data segment_data.json
      --background-color Y --author Z
  → prompt.Engine.Primary()          ANSI string
  → cli/image/image.go               rasterize (fork of homeport/termshot,
                                      fogleman/gg + opentype)
  → website/static/img/themes/X.png
  → append markdown into docs/themes.md
```

Everything that decides what a prompt looks like is Go: [prompt/engine.go](src/prompt/engine.go) (864 lines), [config/segment.go](src/config/segment.go), `segments/*`, `template/`, `color/`, `terminal/writer.go`. `image.go` is 920 lines of rasterizer that exists only because there was no other way to get pixels into markdown.

No WASM build, no JS renderer, no render endpoint. Website has zero of it.

## The wedge already exists

[cli/data.go](src/cli/data.go) — `applyDataFile` sets `flags.SegmentData` + `flags.EnvData`, and segments replay from that instead of shelling out to `git`, `kubectl`, `az`. `segment_data.json` covers every segment.

That makes the engine **hermetic**: no exec, no filesystem walk, no HTTP. That's precisely the property a browser build needs. `--data` was built for screenshots, but it's the studio's foundation.

## Three ways to get it on the web

**1. WASM — single source of truth.** `GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm` build of the engine. With `SegmentData` populated the hot path already avoids exec/fs; cache and HTTP need stubs. Ship the config from the editor, get output back. No drift, ever.

**2. Render endpoint — cheapest.** `website/api` is already Azure Functions ([api/mcp](website/api/mcp), [api/auth](website/api/auth)). Add `/api/render`: POST config + data, shell the real binary, return output. Zero drift, zero WASM work, one round-trip per edit (debounce ~120ms). Also replaces the PNG build step for the gallery.

**3. TypeScript reimplementation — don't.** Template engine, 117 segments, color resolution, palettes, gradients, powerline joining. Guaranteed drift, and the drift is invisible until a user reports a wrong prompt.

## Missing piece either way

Both 1 and 2 return **ANSI**, so the browser needs an ANSI parser — same problem `image.go` already solved badly once.

Better: add a structured emitter alongside the image one. `terminal/writer.go` already tracks foreground, background, and style per run — it just flattens them to escape codes. Emit them instead:

```
config export render --format json --data segment_data.json
→ [{ "text": "alice", "fg": "#191724", "bg": "#eb6f92", "bold": true }, …]
```

Then JS maps runs to spans. No parser, no fidelity guesswork, and it's testable in Go against the same golden files the ANSI writer uses.

**Recommendation:** endpoint + structured export first (small, no drift, unblocks Phase 2–3 of the artifact). WASM later only if the studio needs sub-100ms interactive feedback. That ordering also lets you delete `cli/image/image.go` — 920 lines of rasterizer whose only consumer is the gallery you're replacing.

Customers also use the imager, but it's a good idea to move it entirely to the web because then, with `oh-my-posh-generate-image`, we could also just call the endpoint with a configuration that returns the image itself. I'm actually in favor of having a render endpoint, but not with the binary, but an actual TypeScript implementation, or should you just include a WASM? We then need to have a way to exclude the image render from the binary we ship to people.

content.text:
Two different renderers hiding under one word. They have opposite answers.

| Layer | What it does | Reimplement in TS? |
|---|---|---|
| **Evaluation** | config + context → styled runs. 117 segments, template language, palettes, gradients, powerline joins | **No.** Drift is silent and user-visible |
| **Rasterization** | styled runs → pixels. [image.go](src/cli/image/image.go), 920 lines, forked termshot | **Yes, safely.** Worst case is a pixel diff, not a wrong prompt |

So: TS for the raster, Go for the evaluation. Which means WASM — but read the next part first, because it may make the raster question disappear.

## The imager is already less local than you think

[image.go:236-246](src/cli/image/image.go:236) downloads `Hack.zip` from the nerd-fonts GitHub release at runtime and caches it. `config export image` already requires network on first use. The offline argument against a thin client is weaker than it looks.

And [image.go:462](src/cli/image/image.go:462) shows the layout is a **character grid** — one `spaceAdvance` constant drives measurement, wrapping, and width. Not real typesetting.

## So don't move the imager to the web. Move the rasterizer out of the imager.

Emit **SVG from Go** instead of PNG:

- Grid geometry, one advance constant. ~150 lines.
- Drops `fogleman/gg`, `esimov/stackblur-go`, `golang.org/x/image/font/opentype`, `golang/freetype`, and the Hack.zip download.
- `config export image` stays fully local and gets *faster and more offline* than today.
- SVG is the interchange format for everything else: gallery assets (~2-5KB each vs 8MB of PNG), studio preview, endpoint output.
- PNG becomes a conversion step, done wherever convenient — `resvg-wasm` in the Function, or `--format png` shelling to nothing at all if you decide PNG is a web-only concern.

That reframes your question: you don't need TS-vs-WASM for the imager. You need it for the **studio**, where it's WASM, because the studio needs evaluation.

## Excluding it from the shipped binary

Ranked:

1. **SVG emitter, no exclusion needed.** The deps leave, the feature stays. No build tags, no second artifact, no infra dependency. Do this first.
2. **Build tag** (`//go:build !noimage`) — only worth it if the SVG emitter still costs more than you want. Two artifacts confuses users; you'd have to pick which one is "the" release.
3. **Thin client that POSTs to the endpoint** — last resort. Creates a hard runtime dependency on your infra for a CLI command, and see below.

## Before you build a public render endpoint

**The `http` segment takes an arbitrary URL from config properties** ([segments/http.go:27](src/segments/http.go:27)). So do `owm`, `nba`, `ipify`, `todoist`, `wakatime`. An endpoint that evaluates segments live is an open SSRF proxy — anyone can POST a config that makes your Azure Function fetch internal addresses and return the result.

Non-negotiable if you ship this:

1. **Data-replay only.** Force `flags.SegmentData` populated; hard-disable live segment resolution server-side. Not a config option — a compile-time or entrypoint guard.
2. **Cap and timeout.** Config size limit, template depth limit, render deadline. Gradients and templates are user-supplied compute.
3. **Rate limit per IP.** Unauthenticated image generation is a cheap amplification target.
4. **State the data flow.** Configs and `--data` files carry usernames, hostnames, paths, cloud subscription names. If `config export image` ever POSTs by default, that's a silent behavior change users can't see. Opt-in, or documented loudly.

## Suggested order

1. SVG emitter in Go, behind `config export image --format svg`. Local, no deps, no endpoint.
2. Switch the gallery to SVG. 8MB → ~300KB, crisp, theme-reactive. Delete the PNG pipeline.
3. Drop the rasterizer and its four deps once nothing consumes PNG locally.
4. `GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm` build of the engine — same SVG emitter, now in the browser. This is the studio.
5. Endpoint only if you still want `oh-my-posh-generate-image` as a service — and by then it's the wasm blob in a Function, with the guards above, not a shelled binary.

Steps 1–3 are pure wins with no new infrastructure. Step 4 is where the studio actually starts.

What is the advantage of having it within the binary and not just having a generic builder from a configuration? Alternatively, currently the engine and the writer are all focused around ANSI, but we could create a new writer instead of a separate imaging section or module in the codebase that writes directly to SVG (instead of reusing the same logic but only writing differently).
